passage: I'm Tanvir, and I sit behind Damini in Class 10. For the first two weeks after her brother died, people were so careful. Teachers let her skip homework; the girls walked her to the bus. Then it stopped. Now it's six weeks later and nobody says his name. At lunch they talk about the fest and a new film, and Damini sits there with her tiffin closed. Yesterday someone laughed about a video, and she got up and left. I heard her say to herself on the stairs, 'Like he never existed.' I wanted to say something, but I was scared of making it worse, of making her cry. I think everyone is. I think that's the problem.

qa.q: How long after her brother died is it now?
qa.a: It's six weeks later.

qa.q: What does Damini's 'Like he never existed' reveal about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels alone and even betrayed, as if everyone has forgotten her brother while she is still grieving.

qa.q: What small step could Tanvir or the others take now?
qa.a: Gently say her brother's name or ask, 'Do you want to talk about him?', and let her choose; a trusted teacher or counsellor could also check in.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir think everyone has stopped mentioning the death?
qa.a: He believes they're scared that saying the name will hurt her more or make her cry, so their silence comes from fear, not forgetting.

grounding: A classmate sees a bereaved teenage girl feel alone and betrayed as others stop mentioning her brother, while they stay silent out of fear.

passage:
Week one after the rites. Anirban came every evening to Dolma's house in Darjeeling with notes from school and sat on the steps with her. Sometimes they talked about her Ama; sometimes they didn't talk at all.
Week five. Anirban stopped coming. At school he talked about football and exams, never about Ama. Dolma waited for him to ask how she was. He didn't. That night she wrote in her notebook: Even he's moved on.
Week seven. On the bus she finally asked him, voice shaking, 'Why don't you ever say her name?' Anirban looked at his hands. 'I thought if I did, you'd be sad again. I didn't want to be the one who made you cry.' Dolma stared at him. 'I'm already sad. Saying her name helps.'

qa.q: What did Anirban bring when he came in week one?
qa.a: He brought notes from school.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when she wrote 'Even he's moved on'?
qa.a: She felt alone and betrayed, believing even her close friend had forgotten her Ama.

qa.q: What turning point happens on the bus, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Dolma asks why Anirban never says her mother's name and learns his silence came from fear; telling him that saying it helps lets them grieve together again.

qa.q: What had Anirban been afraid of all those weeks?
qa.a: He was afraid that mentioning her Ama would make Dolma sad again and that he'd be the one who made her cry 🤍.

grounding: Over weeks a bereaved teenage girl feels abandoned as her friend stops mentioning her mother, then learns he stayed silent out of fear.

passage:
By the second month, the school had gone back to normal. Teachers were talking about exams. Jaya's friends talked about a new series. Nobody said "your mother" any more.
In the canteen, Zeenat was telling a funny story. Jaya laughed at the right place. Inside, she felt like she was standing behind a glass wall. Didn't anyone remember? Had they all just forgotten?
Later, walking to class, Zeenat touched her arm. "Jaya, can I say something? I don't mention your Ammi because I'm scared of making you cry."
Jaya stopped. "I'd rather cry," she said. "Than have everyone act like she never existed."
Zeenat nodded slowly and linked arms with her.

qa.q: What did Jaya's friends talk about?
qa.a: A new series.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling behind the glass wall?
qa.a: She felt alone and betrayed, as if everyone had forgotten her mother.

qa.q: What turning point did Zeenat create?
qa.a: By admitting her fear of mentioning Jaya's Ammi, she opened a way for Jaya to say she wants her mother remembered.

qa.q: What had Zeenat been afraid of?
qa.a: Zeenat feared that saying Jaya's Ammi's name would make her cry and hurt her more.

grounding: Shows a grieving teen feeling alone as friends move on and stop mentioning her mother, while a friend admits fearing that saying her name will hurt.

passage:
Dear Sharmila Masi,
It's been six weeks since Papa's funeral. Everyone came for the rites and said, "Call us anytime." Now nobody calls.
At school my friends are normal again. They talk about cricket and exams. When I said "Papa used to take me to matches," everyone went silent and someone changed the subject. It felt like they wanted me to stop.
At home Mummy and I don't talk about him either. I think she's scared I'll cry. I'm scared she'll cry.
You're the only one who still says his name. Can you please keep saying it? I don't want everyone to forget him.
Raghav

qa.q: How long has it been since Papa's funeral?
qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when his friends went silent?
qa.a: Raghav felt alone and hurt, as if they wanted Papa forgotten.

qa.q: What small step could help Raghav at this stage?
qa.a: Masi and Mummy could keep saying Papa's name, and Raghav could tell a trusted friend or teacher he wants to talk about him.

qa.q: What might Raghav's friends be feeling when they change the subject?
qa.a: They may feel awkward and afraid of upsetting Raghav, not realising silence hurts more.

grounding: Shows a grieving teen writing that everyone has moved on and stopped mentioning his father, while others fear mentioning him.

passage:
Samir, you asked me, your friend Amandeep, why I've been skipping lunch with the group. Okay. I'll tell you.
It's been two months since my mother died. For the first two weeks everyone was so kind. Messages, food, hugs. Then it stopped. Now it's like nothing happened. You all talk about the trip, the match, who likes who. And I sit there and think, my mother is gone, and the world just kept going.
I know nobody means it badly. Maybe you're scared to mention her. Maybe you think it'll hurt. But the silence hurts more. It feels like she's being erased.
That's why. I'm not angry with you exactly. I just feel so alone. Her name was Harpreet, by the way. You can say it.

qa.q: How long ago did Amandeep's mother die?
qa.a: Two months ago.

qa.q: What is Amandeep feeling at the group lunches?
qa.a: Amandeep feels alone and hurt, as if the mother who died is being erased while the world keeps going.

qa.q: What could Samir do after hearing this?
qa.a: Say her name, Harpreet, ask about her, and include Amandeep in ways that don't pretend nothing happened.

qa.q: Why might Samir and the others have stopped mentioning her?
qa.a: They may have feared saying her name would hurt Amandeep more, and didn't realise the silence felt worse.

grounding: Shows a grieving teen telling a friend that everyone has moved on and fallen silent about the death, which feels lonelier than mentioning her.

passage:
Two weeks after the rites, the last relatives left. Mausi hugged Vasudha at the station and said, "Be brave, study well." At home, Anand bhaiya's room stayed shut, and nobody said his name at dinner.
A month later, in the school canteen, her friends planned costumes for the annual fest. Kiran began, "Remember when Anand bhaiya did that magic show..." then stopped, went red and talked about glitter instead. Vasudha stared at her tray. It was as if he had been erased and everyone had agreed to it.
On Saturday, sitting on Kiran's terrace, Vasudha finally said it. "You can say his name. I want you to."
Kiran's eyes filled. "I was so scared it would hurt you more."
"It hurts more when nobody does."

qa.q: What did Mausi say at the station?
qa.a: "Be brave, study well."

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel when Kiran stopped mid-sentence in the canteen?
qa.a: She felt alone and betrayed, as if her brother had been erased and everyone had agreed to it.

qa.q: What helped on the terrace?
qa.a: Vasudha said plainly that she wanted to hear his name, which let Kiran stop guessing and speak honestly.

qa.q: Why did Kiran stop mid-story in the canteen?
qa.a: Kiran was scared that mentioning Anand bhaiya would hurt Vasudha more, not uncaring about the loss.

grounding: Shows a bereaved teenager feeling alone and betrayed as others go back to normal and avoid the name, while a friend fears saying it would hurt.
